title: 2.9.5 C Libraries: Using, Compiling, and Linking

questions.q: A C library consists of which two parts?
choices: A main() function and a Makefile
An API defined in header (.h) files, and an implementation usually provided in precompiled binary form
A .s assembly file and a .o object file
A shell script and an executable a.out
questions.explain: The API (function prototypes, types, constants, globals) is in header files. The implementation is often precompiled into a .a archive or a .so shared object that gets linked into the executable.

questions.q: A library's header files define what it exports to its users. They usually contain function prototypes and may also contain type, constant, or global variable declarations.
questions.explain: Headers are the library's API: what users of the library can see and use.

questions.q: A precompiled library file such as libsomelib.a or libsomelib.so can be run directly as a program.
questions.explain: Library binaries are not executable programs. They provide executable code that gets linked into an executable file.

questions.q: A library's implementation may include header files that are internal to it. How do those internal headers relate to the library's API?
choices: They replace the need for function prototypes
They are not part of the API, but they are part of well-designed, modular library code
They must be included by every program that uses the library
questions.explain: Internal headers are used only inside the library's implementation and are not exported to users.

questions.q: What file extension does an archive file have when it contains several .o files that can be statically linked into an executable (for example, libsomelib.?)
questions.explain: Archive files (.a) are statically linked at compile time.

questions.q: Which library file can be dynamically linked into a running program at runtime?
questions.explain: A shared object (.so) file is loaded and linked at runtime. A .a archive is statically linked at compile time.

questions.q: A program that calls functions declared in string.h must add -lstring to the gcc command line.
questions.explain: The string library is part of the standard C library (libc), and gcc links libc into every executable automatically. The program only needs #include <string.h>.

questions.q: The readline library is installed as libreadline.so.8.0. Which gcc option links it in?
questions.explain: The -l argument leaves off the lib prefix, the .so or .a suffix, and any version numbers. That lets gcc pick the most recent version found in the library path.

questions.q: Linking the POSIX threads library is a special case. Which option do you use?
questions.explain: The POSIX threads library is linked with -pthread, without the usual -l prefix. Example: gcc -o myprog myprog.c -pthread -lreadline

questions.q: Both a .so and a .a version of a library are available and you link with -lname. What happens by default, and how do you get static linking?
choices: gcc always links statically. Use --dynamic to get dynamic linking.
gcc may choose to link dynamically. Ask for static linking explicitly, for example with --static.
gcc reports an ambiguity error. You must give the full file name.
gcc links both versions into the executable.
questions.explain: Because -l does not name an exact file, gcc can choose to link dynamically when both versions exist. Static linking must be requested, for example: gcc -o myprog myprog.c --static -pthread -lreadline

questions.q: Which compilation step runs first and expands directives such as #define and #include?
questions.explain: The precompiler (preprocessor) step runs first. It handles the # directives.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the C compilation steps, followed by the step that can happen at runtime?
choices: precompiler, compile, assembly, link editing, runtime linking
compile, precompiler, link editing, assembly, runtime linking
precompiler, assembly, compile, link editing, runtime linking
compile, assembly, precompiler, runtime linking, link editing
questions.explain: Source (.c) goes through the precompiler, then the compiler (.s), then the assembler (.o), then the link editor (a.out). Runtime linking happens only if shared objects were linked in.

questions.q: Which gcc flag stops after the precompiler step so you can see its output?
questions.explain: gcc -E myprog.c prints the preprocessed output. You can redirect it to a file to read it.

questions.q: What does gcc -S myprog.c produce?
choices: myprog.o, a relocatable binary object file
myprog.s, a text file containing the machine-specific assembly translation
Preprocessed C source printed to standard output
questions.explain: The compile step turns C source into assembly code, a human-readable form of machine instructions. -S stops after this step.

questions.q: Which gcc flag stops after the assembly step and produces myprog.o?
questions.explain: gcc -c myprog.c produces the relocatable object file myprog.o.

questions.q: A relocatable object file (.o) contains machine code instructions and is a complete program that can run on its own.
questions.explain: A .o file contains machine code but is not a complete executable. It still has to go through link editing.

questions.q: What is the binary file format that gcc produces on Unix and Linux systems? Give the acronym.
questions.explain: ELF stands for Executable and Linkable Format.

questions.q: Which tool can disassemble the functions in a binary file such as myprog.o or a.out (used with the -d flag)?
questions.explain: objdump -d myprog.o disassembles the functions in the object file.

questions.q: In which step does the linker check that every symbol referenced in a .o file is defined in some .o, .a, or .so file?
questions.explain: The link editing step combines .o files and libraries into a single executable. If it cannot find a symbol's definition, it fails with an undefined-symbol error.

questions.q: At which step would you get an error because gcc cannot find a header file named in an #include directive?
questions.explain: #include is a preprocessor directive, so a missing header is reported during the precompiler step.

questions.q: Which kinds of errors or warnings come from the compile step (C source to assembly)?
choices: Errors from missing definitions and function prototypes
A shared object file that cannot be found when the program starts
questions.explain: The compile step reports C syntax errors, undefined symbol warnings, and missing definition or prototype errors. A missing .so is reported at runtime. Bad preprocessor directive syntax is reported in the precompiler step.

questions.q: When an executable is statically linked against a .a library, how does it get the library's code?
choices: gcc copies the library functions into a.out, and calls to them are bound to those copies inside a.out
a.out records only the library's name, and the code is loaded when the program runs
The library's source code is recompiled every time the program runs
The operating system shares one copy of the .a file with all running programs
questions.explain: Static linking embeds copies of the library functions in a.out. Calls are bound to the addresses where those copies sit in a.out.

questions.q: In this material, what does binding a call to a library function mean?
choices: Adding the function's prototype to a header file
Replacing the use of the function's name with the function's address in memory
Compiling the function into assembly code
questions.explain: Binding associates a name with a location in the program's memory. For a function call, the name is replaced with the function's address.

questions.q: An a.out that was dynamically linked against a .so library contains a copy of that library's function code.
questions.explain: A dynamically linked a.out only records which shared libraries it needs. The library code is loaded and linked at runtime.

questions.q: When does dynamic linking of shared objects take place for a dynamically linked executable?
choices: At runtime, before the program starts executing main
At runtime, the first time main returns
Only when the program is run under GDB
questions.explain: When the program is launched, the system loads the needed .so files and links them in before main begins executing.

questions.q: When a dynamically linked program starts, what does the dynamic linker do?
choices: Examines the executable's list of shared object dependencies
Finds and loads the needed .so files into the running program
Updates relocation table entries to bind the program's uses of shared-object symbols to their locations in the loaded .so files
Permanently copies the library code into the a.out file on disk
questions.explain: The dynamic linker reads the dependency list, loads the shared objects, and updates relocation entries. It does not change a.out on disk or recompile anything.

questions.q: Which utility lists the shared object dependencies of an executable file such as a.out?
questions.explain: ldd a.out lists the shared objects the executable needs.

questions.q: In a header file, what does the extern prefix on the prototype extern int libraryfunc(int x, int y); mean?
choices: The function can only be called from inside the header file
The function's definition is in another file, such as one of the library's .c files
The function is defined as a macro
The function must be linked statically
questions.explain: extern says the function is defined elsewhere, not in the header. Here it is in the library's implementation.

questions.q: A program calls libraryfunc without including its header. gcc prints: warning: implicit declaration of function libraryfunc. Why is this only a warning, not an error?
choices: gcc assumes the function returns an int and keeps compiling
gcc finds the prototype automatically in /usr/include
The linker will supply the missing prototype
Function calls are never checked by the compiler
questions.explain: Without a prototype, gcc assumes an int return type and continues. Don't ignore the warning: it usually means a header with the prototype was not included.

questions.q: If a header that defines the constant MAX is not included, gcc only warns that MAX is undeclared and keeps compiling with a guessed value.
questions.explain: The compiler cannot guess the value of a missing constant, so 'MAX undeclared (first use in this function)' is an error. 'Undeclared' messages often mean a header defining a constant or global variable is missing.

questions.q: The header is included, but compiling gives: myprog.c:9: undefined reference to libraryfunc / collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status. What is the most likely fix?
choices: Add -lexamplelib to the gcc command line
questions.explain: 'undefined reference' comes from the linker (ld). It means the function's implementation was not found, so the library needs to be linked explicitly.

questions.q: Which component of the compiler reports 'undefined reference' errors (it appears in the message 'collect2: error: ... returned 1 exit status')?
questions.explain: ld is the linker component of the compiler.

questions.q: gcc reports: fatal error: examplelib.h: No such file or directory. The header is in /home/me/include. Which option fixes this?
questions.explain: -I adds a directory to the header (include) search path.

questions.q: Linking fails with: /usr/bin/ld: cannot find -lexamplelib. The file libexamplelib.so is in /home/me/lib. Which option fixes this?
questions.explain: -L adds a directory to the linker's library search path. Example: gcc -I/home/me/include -o myprog myprog.c -L/home/me/lib -lexamplelib

questions.q: The program compiled and linked fine, but running it gives: error while loading shared libraries: libexamplelib.so: cannot open shared object file. What fixes this?
choices: Recompile with -I pointing at the library directory
Add the library's directory to the LD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variable
questions.explain: The runtime (dynamic) linker uses LD_LIBRARY_PATH to find .so files. Example: export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/home/me/lib:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

questions.q: Where does gcc look for header files automatically, with no extra options?
questions.explain: Standard headers are commonly in /usr/include, and gcc also searches the current working directory. Other locations need -I. LD_LIBRARY_PATH is for finding .so files at runtime.

questions.q: On many systems, which standard directory holds library files that gcc searches automatically?
questions.explain: Standard libraries are commonly stored in /usr/lib, and gcc searches there by default.
